```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(isw)
library(units)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(sf)
```

## Overview

This vignette presents the main `isw` workflow for estimating stream
depletion and the resulting water-level changes in an aquifer. It compares
the package's two methods for estimating depletion and stream-injection
using spatial inputs included with the package:

* `method = "adf"`, the default, calculates analytical depletion and
  apportions it among stream segments; and
* `method = "constant_head"` solves the injection rates needed to keep
  water-level change equal to zero at the stream-segment model points.

The focus here is how to prepare the inputs and connect the main functions.
For more detail on ADF calculations, see the
[ADF modeling internals](https://gopalpenny.github.io/isw/articles/adf-modeling-internals.html).

## Load the spatial inputs

The package includes a synthetic example domain with two pumping wells, three
connected stream reaches, and two observation wells, all as `sf` objects.

```{r spatial-inputs}
pumping_wells <- example_pumping_wells
stream_reaches <- example_stream_reaches
observation_wells <- example_observation_wells

spatial_inputs_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = stream_reaches, color = "grey65", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_sf(data = pumping_wells, color = "firebrick", shape = 8, size = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = observation_wells, color = "#0072B2", shape = 17, size = 3) +
  geom_sf_text(data = pumping_wells, aes(label = pump_id), nudge_y = 100) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = observation_wells,
    aes(label = observation_id),
    nudge_y = -100
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

spatial_inputs_plot
```

See the
[`prep_stream_segments()` reference](https://gopalpenny.github.io/isw/reference/prep_stream_segments.html)
for CRS requirements, coordinate transformations, and automatic selection of
a projected analysis CRS.

Required identifiers for spatial inputs are `reach_id` (for stream reaches), `pump_id` (for pumping wells), and `observation_id` (for observation wells), respectively.
Pumping wells must also provide aquifer properties as `units` vectors including:
hydraulic conductivity `K`, aquifer thickness `D`, and
drainable porosity `V`. The optional `well_diam` prevents a point-well
singularity when a response is evaluated inside the well radius.

The individual objects and their columns can be inspected directly.

```{r inspect-spatial-inputs}
pumping_wells
stream_reaches
observation_wells
```

## Divide the stream into model segments

Both the `adf` and `constant-head` methods can use the same stream segments object, generated by `prep_stream_segments`.
The `reach_spacing` argument is the
maximum modeled segment length; smaller values represent the stream boundary
at greater spatial resolution but increase the number of injection rates that
must be calculated.

Each returned line is a finite injection element. Its `model_point` is the
reach midpoint, to which the constant-head model is calibrated. `stream_width`
can be supplied as a physical stream width or kept as the
default of 1 m. `stream_width` fixes the near-stream response to that of
`stream_width/2`, and is only used when estimating changes in water level
on or near the stream.

```{r stream-segments}
stream_segments <- prep_stream_segments(
  stream_reaches,
  reach_spacing = set_units(400, "m")
)

stream_segments[c(
  "reach_id",
  "reach_segment_id",
  "represented_length",
  "stream_width"
)]
```

The map below shows the resulting model geometry. Each colored line is one
stream segment, and the white circles mark the segment midpoint collocation
points where the constant-head boundary condition is imposed.

```{r plot-stream-segments}
spatial_inputs_plot +
  geom_sf(
    data = stream_segments,
    aes(color = reach_segment_id),
    linewidth = 2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = stream_segments,
    aes(geometry = model_point),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    color = "black",
    size = 2.5,
    stroke = 0.7
  )
```

## Define pumping and model times

`pumping_schedules` is a wide tibble, with pumping provided as `units` objects.
Its first column, `t`, gives the start of
each pumping period; every other column is named for a `pump_id` and contains
that well's rate. Rates continue until the next schedule row, so a shutdown
at the end must be represented by a row that sets the rate to zero.

```{r pumping-schedule}
pumping_schedules <- tibble(
  t = as.Date(c("2025-01-01", "2025-02-01", "2025-03-01", "2025-04-01")),
  pump_1 = set_units(c(500, 500, 300, 0), "m^3/day"),
  pump_2 = set_units(c(0, 250, 250, 0), "m^3/day")
)

pumping_schedules
```

The `isw` functions generally use `pumping_schedules$t` as default values at
which to generate outputs. But if other times are desired,
`evaluation_times` specifies when stream depletion and
water-level results are
returned.

Pumping-schedule times and evaluation times are always included as
boundaries of the piecewise-constant stream-injection schedule.
The optional `injection_times` argument can add schedule boundaries without
requesting additional water-level output. This can improve the interval-average
approximation to continuously changing ADF depletion, but it increases
computation for both methods. Constant-head rates are solved to satisfy the
boundary at each interval end. Very short intervals can therefore require large
corrective rates, especially when a regular refinement grid is combined with
nearby evaluation or pumping times. This example uses monthly evaluation times
and adds refinement times 5, 10, and 15 days after each pumping-schedule change.
Applications that add refinement times should inspect sensitivity to the
resulting interval lengths.
The `quadrature_order` sets the number of Gauss--Legendre evaluation points on
each positive-length straight section of a stream segment; this example uses
four throughout.

```{r model-times}
evaluation_times <- seq.Date(
  from = as.Date("2025-01-01"),
  to = as.Date("2026-01-01"),
  by = "month"
)

injection_times <- sort(c(
  pumping_schedules$t + 5,
  pumping_schedules$t + 10,
  pumping_schedules$t + 15
))

quadrature_order <- 4
```

See the
[`generate_stream_injection_schedule()` reference](https://gopalpenny.github.io/isw/reference/generate_stream_injection_schedule.html)
for the complete input requirements and interval construction rules.

## Construct both stream-injection schedules

Before the ADF model can be used to estimate stream depletion,
the total analytical depletion for each pumping well must
be apportioned spatially over the stream network.
`prep_adf_stream_apportionment()` calculates a set of
segment weights independently for each pumping well. `sample_spacing`
controls how finely curved stream geometries are sampled when
the segment weights are calculated.

```{r prep-adf-apportionment}
stream_apportionment <- prep_adf_stream_apportionment(
  pumping_wells,
  stream_segments,
  sample_spacing = set_units(100, "m"),
  method = "web_squared"
)
```

To confirm the weights, we can sum the weights, or `apportionment_fraction`,
over all stream segments for each pumping well.

```{r summarize-adf-apportionment}
stream_apportionment |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(pump_id) |>
  summarize(
    total_apportionment_fraction = sum(apportionment_fraction),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Now we can calculate ADF stream depletion directly at the requested times.
This is the simplest route when only ADF depletion, rather than its effect on
aquifer water levels, is needed.

```{r direct-adf-depletion}
adf_depletion <- model_adf_stream_depletion(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  stream_apportionment = stream_apportionment,
  evaluation_times = evaluation_times
)

adf_depletion_totals <- adf_depletion |>
  group_by(pump_id, evaluation_time) |>
  summarize(
    adf_depletion_at_time = sum(stream_depletion_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

adf_depletion_totals
```

These stream depletion values are specific to the requested evaluation times.
In order to model changes in aquifer water levels, we need a schedule of
stream depletion, to be used as stream injection over the entire time range.
This interval schedule is calculated as an additional step for the `"adf"`
model, whereas stream depletion in the `"constant_head"` model is equivalent
to the stream injection schedule.

We can now construct these two interval schedules, using the same function and
time grid. With `method = "adf"`, `generate_stream_injection_schedule()` calls
`model_adf_stream_depletion()` at every schedule boundary and averages depletion
at adjacent boundaries. It reports the resulting `injection_rate` as positive
when water moves from the stream to the aquifer. This rate is the stream-
depletion rate applied over the interval.
Precalculated ADF depletion can be supplied through the
`adf_stream_depletion` argument to avoid recalculation. Here, the supplied
result contains only the monthly evaluation times and omits the optional
refinement boundaries. `generate_stream_injection_schedule()` issues a
warning to make the mismatch explicit, reuses the supplied values, and
fills in the missing times by calculating them within the function.

```{r adf-injection-schedule, warning = TRUE}
adf_schedule <- generate_stream_injection_schedule(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = evaluation_times,
  injection_times = injection_times,
  method = "adf",
  stream_apportionment = stream_apportionment,
  adf_stream_depletion = adf_depletion
)
```

With `method = "constant_head"`, each interval rate is
solved to satisfy the constant-head boundary condition on the `model_point`
for each stream segment at the end of each time interval.

```{r constant-head-injection-schedule}
constant_head_schedule <- generate_stream_injection_schedule(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = evaluation_times,
  injection_times = injection_times,
  method = "constant_head",
  quadrature_order = quadrature_order
)
```

The constant-head result includes two diagnostics. `boundary_residual` is the
signed water-level change remaining at a segment model point after the solve.
`matrix_condition_number` indicates the numerical sensitivity of the system;
`isw` warns when it exceeds \(10^6\). The resulting calculations match
injection for each stream segment to each pumping well. But injection
for each segment must account for injection of all stream segments. `isw`
factorizes once for every aquifer-property combination and reuses
the result for each associated pumping
well. This reduces computation while preserving the depletion response
attributed to each pump.

```{r constant-head-diagnostics}
constant_head_schedule |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(
    maximum_absolute_boundary_residual_m = max(abs(as.numeric(
      set_units(boundary_residual, "m")
    ))),
    maximum_matrix_condition_number = max(matrix_condition_number),
    number_of_aquifer_factorizations = n_distinct(aquifer_id)
  )
```

## Compare stream depletion

`injection_rate` is positive when water leaves the stream and enters the
aquifer. For each pumping well, total stream depletion is therefore the
injection rate summed across all stream segments.

For ADF, the injection schedule contains interval-average analytical depletion. For
constant head, it contains the depletion required to impose the stream
boundary condition at the interval end.

```{r summarize-stream-depletion}
stream_depletion <- bind_rows(
  mutate(adf_schedule, method = "ADF"),
  mutate(constant_head_schedule, method = "Constant head")
) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(method, pump_id, interval_start, interval_end) |>
  summarize(
    stream_depletion_rate = sum(injection_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stream_depletion
```

In addition to differences between the ADF and constant-head approaches,
the direct ADF result at an interval end can differ from the average
rate applied during that interval.

```{r plot-stream-depletion, fig.height = 8}
pumping_schedule_plot_data <- pumping_schedules |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -t,
    names_to = "pump_id",
    values_to = "pumping_rate"
  )

pumping_schedule_plot_data <- bind_rows(
  pumping_schedule_plot_data,
  pumping_schedule_plot_data |>
    group_by(pump_id) |>
    slice_tail(n = 1) |>
    mutate(t = max(evaluation_times)) |>
    ungroup()
)

adf_depletion_plot <- adf_depletion_totals |>
  transmute(
    pump_id,
    interval_end = evaluation_time,
    stream_depletion_rate = adf_depletion_at_time,
    method = "ADF at requested time"
  )

pumping_schedule_plot <- ggplot(
  pumping_schedule_plot_data,
  aes(t, pumping_rate)
) +
  geom_step(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~pump_id, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_date(limits = range(evaluation_times)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Pumping rate") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
  )

stream_depletion_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_step(
    data = stream_depletion,
    aes(interval_start, stream_depletion_rate, color = method),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = adf_depletion_plot,
    aes(interval_end, stream_depletion_rate, color = method),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = adf_depletion_plot,
    aes(interval_end, stream_depletion_rate, color = method),
    size = 2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~pump_id, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_date(limits = range(evaluation_times)) +
  labs(
    x = "Interval end",
    y = "Total stream-depletion rate",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

pumping_schedule_plot / stream_depletion_plot +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3))
```

The following map compares the spatial distribution of the two injection
schedules during May 2025. The positive mapped values represent water moving
from the stream to the aquifer. Each stream segment is colored by its total
injection rate for one pumping well and one method.

```{r map-may-injection-rates, fig.height = 9}
may_date <- as.Date("2025-05-15")

may_injection_rates <- bind_rows(
  mutate(adf_schedule, method = "ADF"),
  mutate(constant_head_schedule, method = "Constant head")
) |>
  filter(interval_start <= may_date, interval_end > may_date) |>
  group_by(method, pump_id, reach_segment_id) |>
  summarize(
    injection_rate = sum(injection_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    injection_rate_m3_day = as.numeric(set_units(
      injection_rate,
      "m^3/day"
    ))
  )

injection_segments <- stream_segments |>
  select(reach_segment_id) |>
  left_join(may_injection_rates, by = "reach_segment_id")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = stream_segments, color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(
    data = injection_segments,
    aes(color = injection_rate_m3_day),
    linewidth = 5,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  facet_grid(method ~ pump_id) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    color = "Injection rate\n(m³/day)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Calculate aquifer drawdown and stream recovery

`model_aquifer_water_level_change()` combines the effects of the physical
pumping wells and stream injection at each observation well and evaluation
time. Supplying a previously calculated injection schedule avoids
recalculating the injection rates. Internally, the function checks
to make sure that the timing of the provided schedule match the
timing that would have otherwise been required if the schedule were calculated
here.

```{r calculate-water-levels}
library(dplyr)
adf_water_levels <- model_aquifer_water_level_change(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  observation_wells = observation_wells,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = evaluation_times,
  stream_injection_schedule = adf_schedule,
  quadrature_order = quadrature_order
) |>
  mutate(method = "ADF")

constant_head_water_levels <- model_aquifer_water_level_change(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  observation_wells = observation_wells,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = evaluation_times,
  stream_injection_schedule = constant_head_schedule,
  quadrature_order = quadrature_order
) |>
  mutate(method = "Constant head")

water_levels <- bind_rows(adf_water_levels, constant_head_water_levels)

water_levels |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(
    method,
    pump_id,
    observation_id,
    evaluation_time,
    pumping_drawdown,
    stream_recovery,
    water_level_change
  )
```

`pumping_drawdown` and `stream_recovery` are reported as positive magnitudes,
while `water_level_change` is their signed net effect: negative values indicate a
decline and positive values indicate a rise in the water table.

We can obtain the water-level change associated with each pump, over time, as follows.

```{r plot-water-levels, fig.height = 8}
water_level_totals <- water_levels |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(method, pump_id, observation_id, evaluation_time) |>
  summarize(
    water_level_change_m = as.numeric(set_units(
      sum(water_level_change),
      "m"
    )),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  water_level_totals,
  aes(evaluation_time, water_level_change_m, color = method)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(observation_id ~ pump_id, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(
    x = "Evaluation time",
    y = "Net water-level change (m)",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The
[`model_aquifer_water_level_change()` reference](https://gopalpenny.github.io/isw/reference/model_aquifer_water_level_change.html)
documents the returned pumping, recovery, and net water-level components.

## Map water-level change along the stream

The stream boundary can also be evaluated directly by treating segment
`model_point` locations as observation wells. These are the locations where
the constant-head condition is imposed and are retained in the stream-
segment object returned by `prep_stream_segments()`. To inspect the response
between model points, `prep_stream_sample_points()` creates additional points
along each segment. The constant-head condition is imposed only at model points, so
water-level changes at the sample points are more likely to deviate.

```{r stream-observation-points}
stream_model_points <- st_sf(
  observation_id = paste0(
    "model_",
    stream_segments$reach_segment_id
  ),
  point_type = "Segment model point",
  geometry = stream_segments$model_point
)

stream_sample_points <- prep_stream_sample_points(
  stream_segments,
  sample_spacing = set_units(100, "m")
) |>
  transmute(
    observation_id = paste0("sample_", sample_point_id),
    point_type = "Sample point"
  )

stream_observation_wells <- bind_rows(
  stream_sample_points,
  stream_model_points
)
```

In the figure below, negative values indicate a decline from
the initial condition. The following calculation sums the two pump-specific
responses at each observation point on May 1, 2025.

```{r calculate-stream-water-levels}
stream_map_time <- as.Date("2025-05-01")

adf_stream_water_levels <- model_aquifer_water_level_change(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  observation_wells = stream_observation_wells,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = stream_map_time,
  stream_injection_schedule = adf_schedule,
  quadrature_order = quadrature_order
) |>
  mutate(method = "ADF")

constant_head_stream_water_levels <- model_aquifer_water_level_change(
  pumping_wells = pumping_wells,
  pumping_schedules = pumping_schedules,
  observation_wells = stream_observation_wells,
  stream_segments = stream_segments,
  evaluation_times = stream_map_time,
  stream_injection_schedule = constant_head_schedule,
  quadrature_order = quadrature_order
) |>
  mutate(method = "Constant head")

stream_water_level_map <- bind_rows(
  adf_stream_water_levels,
  constant_head_stream_water_levels
) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(method, observation_id, evaluation_time) |>
  summarize(
    water_level_change_m = as.numeric(set_units(
      sum(water_level_change),
      "m"
    )),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    stream_observation_wells,
    by = "observation_id"
  ) |>
  st_as_sf()
```

```{r map-stream-water-levels, fig.height = 10}
water_level_limit <- max(abs(
  stream_water_level_map$water_level_change_m
))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = stream_segments, color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(
    data = stream_water_level_map,
    aes(
      fill = water_level_change_m,
      shape = point_type
    ),
    color = "black",
    size = 4.5,
    stroke = 0.35
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#B2182B",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2166AC",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-water_level_limit, water_level_limit)
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Sample point" = 21,
    "Segment model point" = 23
  )) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Net water-level\nchange (m)",
    shape = "Observation type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Finally, we can summarize the distribution of hydraulic-head change by method
and observation type to compare the residuals between model points with those
at the segment model points, where the constant-head condition is imposed.

```{r summarize-stream-water-levels}
stream_water_level_summary <- stream_water_level_map |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(method, point_type) |>
  summarize(
    mean_m = mean(water_level_change_m),
    standard_deviation_m = sd(water_level_change_m),
    minimum_m = min(water_level_change_m),
    maximum_m = max(water_level_change_m),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stream_water_level_summary
```
